study.title: Karnataka groundwater 2024: Safe on average at 68% pumped, but nitrate fails in half of samples and 93 taluks sit beyond Safe
study.summary: CGWB December 2024 factsheet for Karnataka: state-level pumping (68.44%) sits just inside the Safe band, yet nitrate exceeds limits in 49% of samples across 27 districts, fluoride in 18% across 19 districts, and 93 of 237 taluks are Semi-critical, Critical or Over-exploited (60 of them Critical or Over-exploited) — with the over-pumped belt concentrated around Bengaluru, Kolar, Tumkur and Ramanagara. Farming uses ~89% of pumped water.

limitations: No precise coordinates in source: district features are reported reference flags with null geometry, filterable but not plotted as points.
R04/R05 spatial patterns are figure-derived (OCR transcription, medium geography confidence) with figure_only flags.
Saline categorization row is blank in all five assessments: preserved as missing, never zero.
State-level Safe aggregate (68.44%) masks taluk-level stress; 93 taluks sit beyond Safe (60 of them Critical or Over-exploited).
Quality units differ per parameter (uS/cm, mg/L, ppb) and are never interconverted; the headline comparison series uses unitless exceedance percentages.
R06 decorative bubble/emblem deferred as styling only, with a value-based reason.
Management recommendations are proposed guidance (proposed_not_observed), not observed outcomes.

Derived visuals are labelled as such: 'All other uses' (11%) is the remainder of the printed ~89% irrigation share; 'Extractable not yet pumped' (5.33 bcm) is 16.88-11.55 bcm; the Over-Exploited band is drawn to 120% for display only (source definition is >100%, open-ended).
Anomaly burden (CS-district-anomaly-burden) counts list memberships (sporadic spots), not concentrations or district averages; Raichur 5/5 means it appears in all five sporadic lists.

target:dgwr-karnataka-2024-v1:study.analysis: This is the official December 2024 groundwater factsheet for the whole state of Karnataka, published by the Central Ground Water Board. Its headline is a paradox: across the state, pumping sits at 68.44% of the refillable supply, just inside the Safe band (which ends at 70%), yet the water coming up is often unsafe — nitrate fails in almost half of all tested samples across 27 districts — and 93 of the state's 237 taluks are graded Semi-critical, Critical or Over-exploited (60 of them Critical or Over-exploited), with the over-pumped belt concentrated around Bengaluru. Farming uses about 89% of everything pumped, so irrigation efficiency is the biggest lever.

target:dgwr-karnataka-2024-v1:layer:qual.analysis: Nitrate is the quality emergency. Almost half of all tested wells (169 of 345) contain more nitrate than the 45 mg/L limit, and high-nitrate spots appear in 27 districts — the widest spread of any contaminant. Nitrate in groundwater usually comes from fertilizers and sewage, so this is mostly about what happens on the land surface, not the rock itself. Fluoride is next (about 1 in 6 samples, 19 districts), then saltiness (about 1 in 7, 15 districts). Arsenic and uranium each fail in only a handful of samples and a few districts. Important: 'sporadic locations' means scattered wells tested high, not that a whole district's water is bad.

target:dgwr-karnataka-2024-v1:layer:stat.analysis: This is the factsheet's hero map: every one of Karnataka's 237 taluks coloured by its pumping grade — Safe, Semi-critical, Critical or Over-exploited. Most of the state is Safe, but a dense red belt of over-pumped taluks runs across the southeast through the Bengaluru, Kolar, Chikballapur, Tumkur and Ramanagara area, with a smaller red cluster around Chitradurga and Davanagere. Yellow Critical taluks are scattered about, and blue Semi-critical ones sit mostly in the far south. Read this as a pattern, not an address book: individual taluks are not labelled on the printed figure, so use it to see where stress concentrates, then check the charts for exact counts.

target:dgwr-karnataka-2024-v1:layer:sali.analysis: Saltiness (measured as EC) gets its own map, from before the 2023 monsoon. Most of the state sits in the yellow middle band, a salty red cluster covers the north-central interior plus a lobe around Chitradurga, and a fresh blue belt runs along the coast, the Western Ghats and Bidar. The five study-area districts near Bengaluru all sit in the yellow middle — their real problems are fluoride and nitrate, not salt (only Tumkur also flags for saltiness). The two salinity pictures agree: the red map areas match the district list of salty wells, which is reassuring because the lists record scattered bad wells while the map shows district-scale classes.

target:dgwr-karnataka-2024-v1:layer:tren.analysis: Across five assessments from 2017 to 2024, pumping has risen every single time, from 10.34 to 11.55 billion cubic metres, while the state-level grade stays just under the 70% Safe ceiling. The danger bands tell a sharper story: Critical taluks have grown in every assessment (8 to 15), even though the Over-exploited share fell from 26% to 19% — partly because the assessment grew from 176 to 237 taluks, so always read counts and shares together. Behind it all, farming takes about 89% of pumped water, which is why the factsheet pushes micro-irrigation: small efficiency gains on farms move the whole state's water balance.

target:dgwr-karnataka-2024-v1:layer:mana.analysis: Most of Karnataka sits on very hard ancient rock, which holds little water — groundwater lives in cracks and weathered zones, with usable alluvium only in a narrow coastal and stream belt. That geology is why the factsheet's recommendations focus on catching rain where it falls: build harvesting structures especially in hard-rock terrain, revive village tanks for artificial recharge, and expand micro-irrigation, since farming uses about 89% of pumped water. It also says to protect shallow city aquifers from urban and industrial pressure and to enforce the 2020/2023 pumping rules. All of these are proposed actions, not observed results — the panel is a to-do list, not a scorecard.

target_insights.analysis: This is the official December 2024 groundwater factsheet for the whole state of Karnataka, published by the Central Ground Water Board. Its headline is a paradox: across the state, pumping sits at 68.44% of the refillable supply, just inside the Safe band (which ends at 70%), yet the water coming up is often unsafe — nitrate fails in almost half of all tested samples across 27 districts — and 93 of the state's 237 taluks are graded Semi-critical, Critical or Over-exploited (60 of them Critical or Over-exploited), with the over-pumped belt concentrated around Bengaluru. Farming uses about 89% of everything pumped, so irrigation efficiency is the biggest lever.

Nitrate is the quality emergency. Almost half of all tested wells (169 of 345) contain more nitrate than the 45 mg/L limit, and high-nitrate spots appear in 27 districts — the widest spread of any contaminant. Nitrate in groundwater usually comes from fertilizers and sewage, so this is mostly about what happens on the land surface, not the rock itself. Fluoride is next (about 1 in 6 samples, 19 districts), then saltiness (about 1 in 7, 15 districts). Arsenic and uranium each fail in only a handful of samples and a few districts. Important: 'sporadic locations' means scattered wells tested high, not that a whole district's water is bad.

This is the factsheet's hero map: every one of Karnataka's 237 taluks coloured by its pumping grade — Safe, Semi-critical, Critical or Over-exploited. Most of the state is Safe, but a dense red belt of over-pumped taluks runs across the southeast through the Bengaluru, Kolar, Chikballapur, Tumkur and Ramanagara area, with a smaller red cluster around Chitradurga and Davanagere. Yellow Critical taluks are scattered about, and blue Semi-critical ones sit mostly in the far south. Read this as a pattern, not an address book: individual taluks are not labelled on the printed figure, so use it to see where stress concentrates, then check the charts for exact counts.

Saltiness (measured as EC) gets its own map, from before the 2023 monsoon. Most of the state sits in the yellow middle band, a salty red cluster covers the north-central interior plus a lobe around Chitradurga, and a fresh blue belt runs along the coast, the Western Ghats and Bidar. The five study-area districts near Bengaluru all sit in the yellow middle — their real problems are fluoride and nitrate, not salt (only Tumkur also flags for saltiness). The two salinity pictures agree: the red map areas match the district list of salty wells, which is reassuring because the lists record scattered bad wells while the map shows district-scale classes.

Across five assessments from 2017 to 2024, pumping has risen every single time, from 10.34 to 11.55 billion cubic metres, while the state-level grade stays just under the 70% Safe ceiling. The danger bands tell a sharper story: Critical taluks have grown in every assessment (8 to 15), even though the Over-exploited share fell from 26% to 19% — partly because the assessment grew from 176 to 237 taluks, so always read counts and shares together. Behind it all, farming takes about 89% of pumped water, which is why the factsheet pushes micro-irrigation: small efficiency gains on farms move the whole state's water balance.

Most of Karnataka sits on very hard ancient rock, which holds little water — groundwater lives in cracks and weathered zones, with usable alluvium only in a narrow coastal and stream belt. That geology is why the factsheet's recommendations focus on catching rain where it falls: build harvesting structures especially in hard-rock terrain, revive village tanks for artificial recharge, and expand micro-irrigation, since farming uses about 89% of pumped water. It also says to protect shallow city aquifers from urban and industrial pressure and to enforce the 2020/2023 pumping rules. All of these are proposed actions, not observed results — the panel is a to-do list, not a scorecard.

blocks.content: Karnataka pumps 11.55 billion cubic metres a year against 16.88 billion of refillable supply — a **stage of extraction of 68.44%**, just under the 70% ceiling that separates Safe from Semi-critical. Each taluk is graded by that same ratio: use more than 70% and it turns Semi-critical, more than 90% Critical, more than 100% (pumping beyond refill) Over-exploited. By that yardstick 144 of 237 taluks are Safe — but 33 are Semi-critical, 15 Critical and 45 Over-exploited. The state average hides the geography: the over-pumped taluks concentrate in a red belt across the southeast around Bengaluru, Kolar, Chikballapur, Tumkur and Ramanagara.
blocks.headline: Safe on average at 68% pumped — but 93 of 237 taluks sit beyond Safe

metrics.explanation: Yearly pumping divided by yearly refillable supply; under 70% is Safe.
metrics.label: Stage of extraction, 2024

blocks.content: Nitrate exceeds its 45 mg/L limit in **169 of 345 samples (48.99%)** — the highest failure rate of any parameter — with high-nitrate spots in **27 districts**, the widest spread recorded. Think of nitrate as a fingerprint of the surface: it usually washes down from fertilizers and sewage. Fluoride fails in 61 of 345 samples (17.68%, 19 districts) and saltiness in 50 of 345 (14.49%, 15 districts). Arsenic (4 of 125) and uranium (6 of 125) fail rarely but matter most per-well: arsenic appears only in Gadag and Raichur, uranium only in Kolar, Raichur and Tumkur. 'Sporadic locations' is the key qualifier — scattered wells tested high, not whole districts.
blocks.headline: Nitrate fails in half of all samples across 27 districts

blocks.content: Five assessments from 2017 to 2024 trace a slow drift. Pumping has risen **every time** (10.34 → 11.55 bcm) while refill wobbles with rainfall, so the state grade stays Safe but the danger bands grow: Critical taluks climb 8 → 15 without a break. Over-exploited counts look flat (45 → 45) yet their share falls (26% → 19%) because coverage widened from 176 to 237 taluks — read counts and shares together. Derived headroom for 2024 is **5.33 bcm** (16.88 extractable minus 11.55 pumped), a computed remainder, not a printed value.
blocks.headline: Seven years: pumping climbs every time, Critical taluks double

metrics.explanation: Computed remainder of usable supply after pumping; not printed in the source.
metrics.label: 2024 headroom

blocks.content: The two printed maps tell different halves of the story. The taluk-status figure shows the southeastern red belt of over-pumping around Bengaluru; the pre-monsoon salinity map shows a **different red** — salty water across the north-central interior plus a lobe around Chitradurga, with fresh blue along the coast and Ghats. The study districts near Bengaluru sit in the yellow middle band on the salinity map: their problem is fluoride and nitrate, not salt (Tumkur excepted, edging the red lobe). The maps and the district anomaly lists corroborate each other where they should overlap.
blocks.headline: Two reds that do not overlap: pumping stress vs salt

blocks.content: Farming takes **about 89%** of Karnataka's pumped groundwater (the remaining ~11% is a derived remainder), which makes irrigation efficiency the decisive lever — the factsheet explicitly recommends wider micro-irrigation. The setting explains the urgency: most of the state is hard ancient rock holding water only in cracks and weathered zones, across nine aquifer groups, with real alluvium confined to a narrow coastal and stream belt. The remaining recommendations are a proposed to-do list, not results: harvest rainwater especially in hard-rock terrain, revive village tanks, use NAQUIM reports and the Ground Water Year Book locally, protect shallow urban aquifers, and enforce the 2020/2023 extraction rules.
blocks.headline: 89% goes to farms: the lever is irrigation on hard rock
